newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Army weak in picking drill sergants - report.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Army weak in picking drill sergants - report.

text.p: The Army does a slapdash job of selecting its candidates for drill sergeant and makes it difficult to weed out unsuited trainees, an interim report from three lawmakers said Thursday.
The three members of the House National Security Committee were chosen last November to look into complaints of sexual misconduct in the military.

Twelve drill sergants at the Aberdeen Proving Grounds in Maryland have been accused of improper sexual relations with trainees. The scandal has prompted a wide review of the military's programmes to prevent misconduct.

The lawmakers said at a news conference they were concerned the process of selecting drill sergeants was not rigid enough. It was difficult for unsuitable candidates to get out of training without adversely affecting their careers, a black mark not imposed for leaving other training schools.

Representative Tillie Fowler, Florida Republican, said a roomful of drill sergants "broke up laughing" when she asked how they had decided to take the job. Most of them had been assigned to it and did not volunteer, she said.
Only soldiers who volunteer to become drill sergeants face screening or psychological testing, the lawmakers said, and those reviews often were cursory.

Representative Steve Buyer, an Indiana Republican who headed the group, said visits to more training centres and to U.S. bases in Europe were planned for August. Hearings also were possible on the military's training programmes against sexual misconduct and its investigations of the problem.

Representative Jane Harmon, California Democrat, said officers at Fort Leonard Wood and the Aberdeen Proving Grounds believed most of the sexual misconduct problems occurred with trainees held over from one class to another.
